questions.q: A 35-year-old farmer presents with a painless ulcer on his right hand with a black eschar and surrounding non-pitting edema. He reports handling animal hides recently. Gram stain shows large gram-positive bacilli in chains. What is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Ciprofloxacin 500mg twice daily for 60 days
Doxycycline 100mg twice daily for 60 days
Amoxicillin 500mg thrice daily for 60 days
Penicillin G 4 MU IV 4-hourly for 14 days
questions.exp: Cutaneous anthrax (Bacillus anthracis) presents with painless ulcer with black eschar. For non-severe cutaneous anthrax, doxycycline 100mg BD for 60 days is recommended due to potential bioterrorism-related antibiotic resistance concerns. Ciprofloxacin is the alternative. IV penicillin is used for systemic disease.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with annular scaly plaques on her trunk. KOH examination shows hyphae. She was prescribed terbinafine 250mg/day for tinea corporis. After 4 weeks, the lesions are not responding. Culture reveals Trichophyton concentricum. What characteristic finding on KOH would suggest this organism?
opts: Thick-walled macroconidia with transverse septa
Concentric rings of hyphae within the stratum corneum
Arthrospores within and around hair shafts (endothrix)
Clusters of budding yeast with short hyphae (spaghetti and meatballs)
questions.exp: Trichophyton concentricum causes tinea imbricata (Tokelau), characterized by concentric rings of scaling on the skin. KOH shows hyphae arranged in concentric rings within the stratum corneum. This organism is uniquely responsible for this morphological pattern seen in Pacific islanders and South Americans.

questions.q: A 6-year-old child presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base around the lips. The mother mentions this is the third episode in 6 months, always triggered by fever. Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells. The child's mother asks about prophylaxis. Which is the most appropriate prophylactic regimen?
opts: Topical acyclovir 5% cream applied 5 times daily indefinitely
Oral acyclovir 400mg twice daily for 6-12 months
Oral valacyclovir 500mg once daily for 6-12 months
Oral famciclovir 250mg twice daily for 6 months
questions.exp: Recurrent herpes labialis occurring ≥6 times per year warrants suppressive therapy. In children, oral acyclovir 400mg BD for 6-12 months is appropriate. Valacyclovir 500mg OD is used in adults. Topical acyclovir has limited efficacy for recurrences. Famciclovir is not routinely used in young children.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man from Bihar presents with hypopigmented patches with loss of sensation. Slit-skin smear from the lesion shows Bacterial Index (BI) of 3+. Histopathology shows foamy macrophages packed with acid-fast bacilli, forming globi. What type of leprosy does this represent, and what is the recommended treatment?
opts: Borderline tuberculoid (BT) leprosy; 6 months paucibacillary MDT
Lepromatous leprosy (LL); 12 months multibacillary MDT
Mid-borderline (BB) leprosy; 12 months multibacillary MDT
Borderline lepromatous (BL) leprosy; 12 months multibacillary MDT
questions.exp: BI of 3+ with foamy macrophages (Virchow cells) packed with globi (bundles of AFB) is pathognomonic of lepromatous leprosy (LL). This is at the anergic pole of the Ridley-Jopling spectrum. Treatment: WHO multibacillary MDT (rifampicin 600mg monthly + clofazimine 300mg monthly + dapsone 100mg daily + clofazimine 50mg daily) for 12 months.

questions.q: A 25-year-old sexually active woman presents with a painful genital ulcer with an undermined edge and a necrotic base. Inguinal lymphadenopathy is present with fluctuant bubo. Gram stain of ulcer exudate shows 'school of fish' pattern with gram-negative coccobacilli. The causative organism is:
opts: Treponema pallidum
Haemophilus ducreyi
Klebsiella granulomatis
Chlamydia trachomatis L1-L3
questions.exp: Chancroid (caused by Haemophilus ducreyi) presents with painful genital ulcers with undermined, ragged edges and necrotic base, associated with painful fluctuant inguinal bubo. The 'school of fish' or 'railroad track' pattern on Gram stain is characteristic. Treatment: azithromycin 1g single dose or ceftriaxone 250mg IM single dose.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with photosensitive butterfly rash on the malar area, oral ulcers, and joint pain. ANA is positive (1:320, homogeneous pattern). Anti-dsDNA antibodies are elevated. She develops worsening renal function. Which finding on renal biopsy would indicate the most severe form of lupus nephritis requiring aggressive immunosuppression?
opts: Mesangial hypercellularity with IgG deposits (Class II)
Focal proliferative changes affecting <50% of glomeruli (Class III)
Diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis affecting >50% of glomeruli (Class IV)
Membranous pattern with subepithelial deposits (Class V)
questions.exp: Class IV (diffuse proliferative) lupus nephritis is the most severe form, affecting >50% of glomeruli with endocapillary proliferation, 'wire loop' lesions, and subendothelial deposits. It carries the worst renal prognosis and requires induction therapy with cyclophosphamide (NIH protocol) or mycophenolate mofetil plus high-dose steroids.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man presents with tense bullae on normal-appearing and erythematous skin, predominantly on the thighs, abdomen, and axillae. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 deposition at the dermoepidermal junction. The target antigen is located on:
opts: Desmoglein 3 (intracellular domain)
NC16A domain of BP180 (collagen XVII)
Desmoglein 1 (extracellular domain)
Type VII collagen (dermal anchoring fibrils)
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid (BP) is characterized by tense bullae with linear IgG/C3 at the DEJ on DIF. The primary autoantigen is the NC16A (non-collagenous) domain of BP180 (BPAG2/collagen XVII), a transmembrane hemidesmosomal protein. BP230 (BPAG1) is the secondary antigen. Desmoglein 3 is the target in pemphigus vulgaris.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man presents with a pearly, translucent nodule with telangiectatic vessels on his nose. Dermoscopy shows arborizing blood vessels, blue-gray ovoid nests, and leaf-like structures. Biopsy confirms the diagnosis. What is the most reliable surgical margin for this tumor to minimize recurrence?
opts: Simple excision with 2mm margins
Simple excision with 4mm margins
Mohs micrographic surgery
Punch excision with 3mm margins
questions.exp: Nodular basal cell carcinoma (BCC) on the nose (H-zone) is a high-risk location. Mohs micrographic surgery (MMS) offers the highest cure rate (99%) with maximum tissue conservation by real-time margin evaluation. For high-risk BCCs (H-zone, >2cm, recurrent, infiltrative), MMS is the treatment of choice over standard excision.

questions.q: During a punch biopsy procedure on the back, at what angle should the punch be held relative to the skin surface for optimal specimen quality?
opts: 45° to the skin surface in the direction of relaxed skin tension lines (RSTLs)
90° perpendicular to the skin surface, rotating in the direction of hair follicle orientation
30° angle to maximize inclusion of subcutaneous tissue
Parallel to Langer's lines to minimize scarring
questions.exp: Punch biopsy should be held at 90° perpendicular to the skin surface to ensure full-thickness skin sampling (epidermis, dermis, subcutis). The punch should be rotated in the direction of hair follicle orientation to avoid transecting follicles obliquely. Stretching skin perpendicular to RSTLs creates an elliptical defect that heals better.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman on long-term isotretinoin for nodulo-cystic acne develops severe myalgia and elevated CK levels. Which investigation should be done before initiating isotretinoin in athletes?
opts: Liver function tests only
Fasting lipid profile only
CK levels, liver function tests, and fasting lipid profile
Complete blood count only
questions.exp: Before starting isotretinoin, baseline investigations should include: liver function tests (hepatotoxicity risk), fasting lipid profile (hypertriglyceridemia risk), and CK levels in athletes/those with physical exertion (rhabdomyolysis risk). Pregnancy test is mandatory in women. CBC is not routinely required but may be done for baseline.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man presents with well-demarcated, erythematous, silvery scaly plaques on his elbows and knees. Auspitz sign is positive. Histopathology of the lesion would characteristically show:
opts: Spongiosis, parakeratosis, and eosinophil infiltration in the epidermis
Regular acanthosis, parakeratosis, Munro microabscesses, and dilated capillaries in dermal papillae
Suprabasal acantholysis with tombstone row of basal cells
Subepidermal blister with eosinophils and neutrophils
questions.exp: Histopathology of psoriasis shows: regular acanthosis (elongated rete ridges), parakeratosis, loss of granular layer, Munro microabscesses (neutrophils in stratum corneum), spongiform pustules of Kogoj, and dilated tortuous capillaries in elongated dermal papillae (explaining Auspitz sign). These are hallmark features.

questions.q: A 2-year-old child presents with intensely pruritic, weeping, crusted lesions on the cheeks and extensor surfaces of limbs. The mother has asthma. Total serum IgE is markedly elevated. This child has atopic dermatitis. Which finding would indicate a higher risk of persistent disease into adulthood?
opts: Onset before 2 years of age
Early onset (<2 years), severe disease, and concurrent food allergy
Male sex and urban residence
Elevated total IgE alone
questions.exp: Risk factors for persistent atopic dermatitis into adulthood include: early onset with severe disease, concurrent food allergy (especially peanut/egg), associated asthma or allergic rhinitis, high total IgE, and family history of atopy. The combination of early onset + severity + food allergy has the strongest predictive value for persistence.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with irregular, depigmented macules on her face and hands since childhood. Wood's lamp examination shows milk-white fluorescence with accentuation of the lesion. Histopathology shows absent melanocytes. She is distressed. The first-line treatment in a non-segmental vitiligo patient with stable disease (<2 years) affecting <10% BSA is:
opts: Narrowband UVB phototherapy (NB-UVB) thrice weekly
Topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus 0.1%) twice daily
Topical corticosteroids (class II-III) for 3 months
Systemic oral minipulse dexamethasone
questions.exp: For limited stable vitiligo (<10% BSA), first-line treatment is topical corticosteroids (mid-to-high potency). Tacrolimus 0.1% is preferred for face and flexures to avoid steroid side-effects. NB-UVB is first-line for widespread (>10% BSA) or unresponsive limited disease. Oral minipulse is for rapidly progressive (unstable) vitiligo.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with diffuse non-scarring hair loss. Pull test: positive. Trichoscopy shows yellow dots, black dots, broken hairs, exclamation mark hairs, and tapering hairs. The most likely diagnosis and the pathological finding on scalp biopsy are:
opts: Androgenetic alopecia; miniaturization of follicles with fibrous streamers
Alopecia areata; peribulbar lymphocytic infiltration ('swarm of bees')
Trichotillomania; pigment casts and fractured hairs without inflammation
Telogen effluvium; increased telogen:anagen ratio >20%
questions.exp: Alopecia areata shows characteristic trichoscopy findings: yellow dots (empty follicles with sebum), black dots (broken hair in follicle), exclamation mark hairs (dystrophic anagen hairs), and short vellus hairs. Biopsy shows lymphocytic infiltrate around anagen bulbs ('swarm of bees'). Peribulbar inflammation is the hallmark.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis presents with firm, non-tender subcutaneous nodules on her elbow and a well-defined erythematous-to-brown plaque with central clearing on her shin. Biopsy of the shin lesion shows palisading histiocytes surrounding a central zone of necrobiosis. The diagnosis is:
opts: Necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum
Granuloma annulare
Rheumatoid nodule
Erythema nodosum
questions.exp: Granuloma annulare (GA) presents with annular plaques with central clearing on acral sites. Histopathology shows palisading or interstitial histiocytes surrounding areas of altered collagen/mucin (necrobiosis). GA is associated with diabetes (generalized form). Necrobiosis lipoidica shows more extensive necrobiosis with lipid deposits, typically on the shins of diabetics.

questions.q: A 20-year-old man presents with recurrent oral erosions and superficial erosions on the chest and back. The blisters rupture easily ('fragile bullae'). Nikolsky sign is positive. DIF shows IgG deposition in an 'fishnet/chicken-wire' pattern throughout the epidermis. Which antigen is primarily targeted?
opts: BP180 (Collagen XVII)
Desmoglein 1
Desmoglein 3
Envoplakin and periplakin
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris (PV) involves suprabasal acantholysis. Mucosal disease involves desmoglein 3 (Dsg3) antibodies. Cutaneous involvement adds desmoglein 1 (Dsg1) antibodies. The primary target in mucosal-dominant PV is Dsg3. DIF shows intercellular IgG/C3 in a 'fishnet' pattern. Envoplakin/periplakin are targeted in paraneoplastic pemphigus.

questions.q: A 70-year-old man presents with a firm, painless, pigmented nodule on his scalp that has grown rapidly over 3 months. Dermoscopy shows a multicomponent pattern with irregular blotches, atypical network, and blue-white structures. Biopsy confirms melanoma. Sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) is indicated if Breslow thickness is:
opts: >0.5mm without ulceration
≥0.8mm with ulceration OR ≥1.0mm regardless of ulceration
>0.75mm with any mitosis
>2mm regardless of other features
questions.exp: Per AJCC 8th edition guidelines, SLNB is indicated for: T1b (0.8-1mm with ulceration or ≥1mm), T2-T4 melanomas. Specifically, SLNB is considered for Breslow thickness ≥0.8mm. For T1b (<0.8mm with ulceration or mitoses), SLNB may be offered. T1a (<0.8mm, no ulceration) does not routinely require SLNB.

questions.q: A dermatologist is performing a chemical peel with 35% trichloroacetic acid (TCA) on a patient. The peel is applied and a white frost appears uniformly over the treated area. The frost pattern observed indicates:
opts: Level 1 frost (erythema with white streaks) — superficial peel reaching upper dermis
Level 2 frost (white coating with erythema showing through) — superficial to mid-papillary dermis
Level 3 frost (solid white with no erythema) — reaching mid-to-deep reticular dermis
No frost means insufficient penetration; continue applying
questions.exp: TCA peel frosting levels: Level 1 = erythema with white streaks (papillary dermis); Level 2 = white coating with pink/erythema showing through (papillary to upper reticular dermis); Level 3 = solid white frost with no erythema (deep reticular dermis). Level 3 frost with 35% TCA indicates a medium-to-deep peel with risk of scarring — endpoint for ablative peeling.

questions.q: A 30-year-old HIV-positive man (CD4 count 120 cells/μL) presents with painful, punched-out oral ulcers and esophageal ulcers. Cultures are negative for bacteria and fungi. CMV PCR is positive. What drug is used to treat CMV esophagitis in HIV?
opts: Acyclovir 800mg five times daily
Ganciclovir 5mg/kg IV twice daily for 21 days
Foscarnet 90mg/kg IV twice daily
Valganciclovir 450mg twice daily for 7 days
questions.exp: CMV esophagitis/colitis in immunocompromised patients (CD4<50) is treated with IV ganciclovir 5mg/kg BD for 14-21 days. Valganciclovir (oral prodrug of ganciclovir) 900mg BD is an alternative for non-severe CMV disease. Foscarnet is used when ganciclovir resistance is suspected. Acyclovir has no efficacy against CMV.

questions.q: A 38-year-old man presents with a hypopigmented, well-defined patch on his left forearm. Sensory testing shows reduced thermal and pain sensation within the patch. Nerve examination reveals thickened ulnar nerve. Slit-skin smear BI = 0. Based on the Ridley-Jopling classification, this is classified as TT (tuberculoid) leprosy. What histopathological finding differentiates TT from BT leprosy?
opts: Absence of lymphocytes in TT vs. prominent lymphocytes in BT
Epithelioid granulomas eroding the epidermis (reaching the basement membrane) in TT vs. grenz zone in BT
Foamy macrophages in TT vs. epithelioid granulomas in BT
No AFB in either TT or BT leprosy
questions.exp: In TT leprosy, well-formed epithelioid granulomas extend up to (and erode) the epidermis/basement membrane — a 'naked' epidermis characteristic. In BT leprosy, there is a clear grenz zone (uninvolved subepidermal zone) between the epidermis and granulomas. This distinction is key on histopathology.

questions.q: A 22-year-old sexually active man presents with a painless, indurated, clean-based ulcer on the glans penis for 2 weeks. Inguinal lymph nodes are non-tender, rubbery. Dark-field microscopy of the ulcer exudate shows motile spirochetes. VDRL titre is 1:8. What is the treatment of choice?
opts: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose
Doxycycline 100mg twice daily for 14 days
Azithromycin 2g orally single dose
Ceftriaxone 250mg IM single dose
questions.exp: Primary syphilis (painless chancre with rubbery lymphadenopathy, positive dark-field microscopy) is treated with benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose — drug of choice. Doxycycline 100mg BD for 14 days is the alternative in penicillin-allergic patients. Azithromycin 2g is a secondary alternative but resistance is emerging. Treatment also covers secondary syphilis.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman on methotrexate for psoriasis develops rapidly progressive worsening of erythema and scaling over her entire body. She becomes febrile (38.8°C), has bilateral leg edema, and her heart rate is 110 bpm. What is the most likely diagnosis and immediate management?
opts: Methotrexate toxicity — stop MTX, give leucovorin rescue
Erythrodermic psoriasis — admit, supportive care, taper MTX
Erythrodermic psoriasis — admit, IV fluids, electrolytes, nutritional support, systemic steroids cautiously
Drug reaction — stop MTX, start systemic cyclosporine
questions.exp: Erythrodermic psoriasis is a dermatological emergency with >90% BSA involvement. Management: hospitalization, IV fluids and electrolyte correction, high-calorie nutrition (increased losses), temperature regulation, emollients. Systemic steroids are contraindicated (risk of rebound). Biologics (infliximab, secukinumab) or cyclosporine are preferred for rapid control. MTX triggers should prompt temporary suspension.

questions.q: A 65-year-old woman presents with hemorrhagic bullae on her lower limbs following a minor trauma. She has a history of chronic kidney disease. Histopathology shows subepidermal blister with few inflammatory cells, and DIF reveals IgA linear deposition at the DEJ. The most likely diagnosis is:
opts: Bullous pemphigoid
Linear IgA bullous dermatosis
Dermatitis herpetiformis
Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita
questions.exp: Linear IgA bullous dermatosis (LABD) shows linear IgA at the DEJ on DIF — the hallmark. It can be idiopathic or drug-induced (commonest: vancomycin, furosemide). Clinical: tense bullae ('string of pearls' arrangement), predominantly in elderly or children. Treatment: dapsone is first-line. Unlike DH, IgA deposits are linear, not granular.

questions.q: A 50-year-old man presents with a flesh-colored, dome-shaped nodule on the ear helix that has grown rapidly over 6 weeks to 2cm, then appears to be regressing centrally with a keratin-filled crater. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Observe for 6 months as spontaneous resolution is expected
Surgical excision with 5mm margins to rule out squamous cell carcinoma
Intralesional 5-fluorouracil injection
Curettage and electrodesiccation
questions.exp: Keratoacanthoma (KA) is a rapidly growing, crateriform tumor with central keratin plug. Despite tendency for spontaneous regression, excision with margin analysis is recommended as KA cannot be reliably distinguished from well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) clinically or histologically in many cases — especially on the ear (high-risk site). Standard excision is preferred.

questions.q: A patient undergoes sclerotherapy for varicose veins. During the procedure, 3% sodium tetradecyl sulfate is injected. Post-procedure, the patient develops a burning sensation and skin necrosis at the injection site. What is the most likely cause?
opts: Hypersensitivity reaction to sclerosant
Extravasation of sclerosant into surrounding tissue
Intra-arterial injection of sclerosant
Air embolism from foam sclerotherapy
questions.exp: Intra-arterial injection of sclerosant is a serious complication causing severe burning, arterial spasm, and distal necrosis (digital or skin necrosis). It requires immediate management: stop injection, aspirate, inject saline/lidocaine, heparin, and prostaglandin E1. Extravasation causes local necrosis but less severe than intra-arterial. Anaphylaxis to STS is rare.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman is started on dapsone for dermatitis herpetiformis. 3 weeks later, she develops pallor, fatigue, and jaundice. CBC shows hemolytic anemia with Heinz bodies on peripheral smear. Her G6PD level is severely deficient. Dapsone causes hemolysis through:
opts: Direct oxidative damage to spectrin causing spherocytosis
Formation of hydroxylamine metabolite causing oxidative hemoglobin denaturation
Immune-mediated IgG coating of red blood cells
Inhibition of dihydropteroate synthetase in RBCs
questions.exp: Dapsone-induced hemolysis occurs via its hydroxylamine metabolite (formed by CYP2C19/CYP3A4) which oxidizes hemoglobin to methemoglobin and generates reactive oxygen species, causing RBC membrane damage (Heinz body formation) and hemolysis. G6PD deficiency worsens this as these patients cannot detoxify oxidative stress via glutathione pathway.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man with scleroderma has significant calcinosis cutis on his fingers with painful nodules and occasional white chalky discharge. What calcium compound is deposited in calcinosis cutis in scleroderma?
opts: Calcium oxalate (dystrophic calcification)
Hydroxyapatite and calcium carbonate-apatite (dystrophic calcification)
Calcium pyrophosphate (metastatic calcification)
Calcium phosphate due to elevated serum levels (metastatic)
questions.exp: Calcinosis cutis in scleroderma is a dystrophic calcification (normal serum calcium/phosphate). The deposits consist primarily of hydroxyapatite [Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2] and calcium carbonate-apatite. This distinguishes it from metastatic calcification (elevated serum calcium × phosphate product) where calcium phosphate and carbonate deposit in normal tissue.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman presents with erythematous vesicular rash in a dermatomal distribution along T4 on the left side. She reports severe burning pain for 3 days before the rash appeared. She is 28 weeks pregnant. What is the safest antiviral treatment for herpes zoster in pregnancy?
opts: Oral valacyclovir 1000mg three times daily for 7 days
Oral acyclovir 800mg five times daily for 7 days
Oral famciclovir 500mg three times daily for 7 days
Intravenous acyclovir 10mg/kg every 8 hours
questions.exp: Acyclovir is pregnancy category B (most studied in pregnancy) and is considered safe. Oral acyclovir 800mg 5×/day for 7 days is recommended for uncomplicated herpes zoster in pregnancy. Valacyclovir is also safe (prodrug of acyclovir) but less studied in pregnancy. IV acyclovir is reserved for disseminated/ophthalmic zoster or immunocompromised patients.

questions.q: A 12-year-old boy presents with scaling of the scalp with broken hairs. Wood's lamp shows dull green fluorescence. KOH of broken hairs shows arthrospores covering the outer surface of hair shafts. The causative organism and type of hair invasion are:
opts: Trichophyton tonsurans; endothrix invasion (arthrospores inside hair shaft)
Microsporum canis; ectothrix invasion (arthrospores outside hair shaft)
Trichophyton violaceum; endothrix, causing black-dot ringworm
Trichophyton schoenleini; favic invasion with air channels
questions.exp: Microsporum canis causes tinea capitis with ectothrix pattern (arthrospores arranged outside the hair shaft). Wood's lamp shows bright green-yellow fluorescence (due to pteridine production). M. audouinii also shows ectothrix with fluorescence. Trichophyton species (tonsurans, violaceum) show endothrix (spores inside hair) with no fluorescence.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman presents with Raynaud's phenomenon, dysphagia, and skin tightening on the face and hands. ANA is positive in a nucleolar pattern. Anti-Scl-70 antibody is positive. What is her risk for developing pulmonary fibrosis?
opts: Low risk; anti-Scl-70 is associated with isolated pulmonary arterial hypertension
High risk; anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) is strongly associated with diffuse cutaneous SSc and ILD
Moderate risk; only ACA (anti-centromere) predicts pulmonary fibrosis
Anti-Scl-70 has no correlation with pulmonary involvement
questions.exp: Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) antibodies are associated with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis (dcSSc) and carry a high risk (~40-60%) of interstitial lung disease (ILD/pulmonary fibrosis). Anti-centromere antibody (ACA) is associated with limited cutaneous SSc (CREST syndrome) and pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), not primarily ILD.

questions.q: A 25-year-old man presents with multiple flesh-colored papules around the anus and perianal region. HPV DNA typing confirms HPV type 6. He is worried about malignant transformation. The most accurate statement regarding HPV-associated anal condylomata acuminata is:
opts: HPV 6 and 11 (low-risk) cause condylomata with <1% malignant transformation risk
HPV 6 causes condylomata with 15% risk of transformation to anal SCC
HPV 16/18 exclusively cause condylomata acuminata
All perianal HPV lesions carry equal malignant potential
questions.exp: HPV types 6 and 11 are low-risk (non-oncogenic) types responsible for >90% of condylomata acuminata (genital warts). Their malignant transformation potential is extremely low (<1%). High-risk HPV types 16, 18, 31, 33 are associated with dysplasia and malignant transformation. Buschke-Lowenstein tumor (giant condyloma) is associated with HPV 6/11 but is locally destructive, not truly malignant.
